I set six places for my grandmother's birthday lunch and checked them twice. The plates matched, the flowers stood in the centre and every chair had enough ____1____. Then Dad arrived with an old friend of Grandmother's who had come unexpectedly to town. I saw the extra person as a problem with my perfect ____2____. Dad saw a chance for two friends to meet. Before I could object, Grandmother stood up with a delighted ____3____. The table needed changing, but the day had already become ____4____. I began looking for another ____5____.

The spare one was lower and did not match. I suggested moving the visitor to a small side table. Grandmother asked whether she should sit there too, since they would have so much to ____6____. I understood her gentle point. A matching arrangement was less important than keeping people ____7____. We moved the flowers, shifted the plates and brought a cushion for the low chair. The table became a little crowded but much more ____8____. I found myself laughing at a story I had never heard about Grandmother's school days. The extra place had added more than another ____9____. It had brought part of her past into the ____10____.

After lunch, the visitor helped me carry plates to the kitchen. She thanked me for making room, without knowing how reluctantly I had begun. I was glad I had time to change my response before it became an unkind word. My careful preparation had not been ____11____. It had simply met something it could not have predicted. The useful skill was not defending the original plan but knowing which part could ____12____. I kept the photograph Dad took: seven people around six matching plates and one different one. The uneven detail did not spoil it. It told the story of a welcome. Now I still count places before a family meal, but I leave room in my thinking for the ____13____. A good table is an arrangement of objects; a good lunch is an encounter between ____14____. I had made the first carefully and nearly forgotten the ____15____.
